Permafrost does not prevent construction, it just makes it cost a bit more. Example, when building a road, we need to blast away all the permafrost we encounter with explosives and build a solid foundation for the road. Its like building a bridge over water. The foundation pillars are whats holding the road/bridge and they are anchored directly onto the bed rock beneath the permafrost. No matter how much the permafrost shifts, melts or reforms, it won't damage the road because the permafrost is not holding the road, its the pillars that are holding it. 
Canada is a lot more advanced then most think. Of course we don't build such roads everywhere, only the most important highways are built like that. For example, the railway upgrade that goes to Churchill is being built this way. 
Now as for farmland, Canada has a lot more then what is currently being farmed. Only the flat lands are being farmed as they are the easiest. But the Canadian Shield has the perfect conditions for farming too. It holds over 20% of the world's fresh water. There is over a million lakes in there. The soil is very fertile, but its small patches here and there. The land needs a lot of manual work. The soil needs to be gathered and terraces needs to be built to hold the soil in place so that farming on a large scale becomes possible. We could even have rice fields because fresh water that abondant. We just need to reshape the land into the shape of terraces. But almost no one wants to do it because Canada already produces too much food as it is.

replies.author: @foilhat1138
replies.text:
@renstein8210 Saying 'just make them, it isn't hard' is peak armchair general ignorance. Turkey didn't build an independent jet because it was 'easy', they spent decades and billions of dollars trying to copy airframes because the US kicked them out of the F-35. Even with all that spending, Turkey’s 'indigenous' KAAN fighter jet literally flies on American General Electric engines, and the US Congress blocked Turkey from exporting it. Their new ATAK 2 attack helicopter runs on Ukrainian engines. They didn't bypass the global supply chain, they are entirely shackled to it.

Furthermore, thinking Canada is unique for having long procurement debates proves you don't follow global defense. The US military spent over 20 years in bureaucratic gridlock over the F-35. And guess what? When the US needs to move fast, they buy foreign, their MH-139 Grey Wolf helicopter is an Italian design, and the Lakota is a European Airbus design. No middle power nation 'just builds' a 5th generation stealth fighter from scratch for a tiny domestic fleet of 88 jets. It would bankrupt the country. We buy the F-35 allied frame, plug 110+ Canadian aerospace contractors into the global build, and win the high margin tech contracts. That is how the actual industry operates.

replies.author: @foilhat1138
replies.text:
@renstein8210 Are you intentionally being this dense, or do you genuinely not know what Canada manufactures? Asking why we don't build air defense, drones, or radars for Ukraine is hilarious because we literally do. Canada's Telemus Systems builds advanced drone warfare suites, Rheinmetall Canada builds air defense systems and radar integrations in Quebec, and L3Harris Wescam in Ontario produces the MX-Series optical radar/targeting pods that are critical to Ukraine’s drone fleet. We don't build generic artillery missiles because we focus on high value electronic warfare, targeting, and drone tech.

Using Russia as some sort of benchmark for independent manufacturing is a joke. They are completely dependent on China just to keep their factories open, and their "advanced" hardware is so hollowed out that it is routinely found packed with smuggled Western consumer chips and components.

replies.author: @foilhat1138
replies.text:
@renstein8210 You're conflating the final assembly of a jet or hull with Canada's actual, highly advanced aerospace and defense manufacturing output. The reality is that no nation, including the US, builds 100% of its military assets entirely in isolation anymore. For starters, we absolutely build our own massive warships. We are currently constructing our entire surface fleet here, including the River class Destroyers in Halifax, alongside new Joint Support Ships and heavy polar icebreakers. 

On the aerospace side, Bombardier builds the Global 6500 military aircraft in Toronto and Montreal, and our domestic companies are so deeply embedded in global supply chains that every single F-35 fighter jet flying today relies on Canadian made components and software. Canada focuses heavily on high margin tech rather than just bending metal for basic frames. We are world leaders in military flight simulators through CAE, space based defense sensors through MDA, and advanced naval weapon systems. You have no idea how defense procurement works.
